query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (2–4 at%) of aluminum to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, protective alumina scale on the surface.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by incorporating 2–4 at% Al via arc-melting synthesis.
generation.conditions: Oxidation testing in air at ~800 °C for 5 hours, along with mechanical evaluations at room temperature and at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al₂O₃) scale on the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong affinity for oxygen and, when added in minor amounts, is expected to segregate to the surface during high-temperature exposure, leading to the in-situ formation of an alumina scale. This oxide acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress, thereby reducing further oxidation while largely preserving the alloy’s mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated material, the Al-modified alloy will show significantly improved oxidation resistance (evidenced by reduced weight gain and enhanced scale integrity) after 5-hour exposure at 800 °C, while maintaining its useful room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which shows acceptable mechanical properties but inadequate oxidation resistance for high-temperature applications.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys exposed in ambient air at ~800 °C for up to 5 hours and evaluated under high-temperature mechanical testing conditions (e.g., tensile tests at 1000 °C with strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum content within the 2–4 at% range and its potential interactions with other alloy constituents may affect both the oxidation behavior and mechanical performance, and these effects require further detailed experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set of untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and one set with an added 2–4 at% Al via standard arc-melting synthesis. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Post-exposure, perform microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM/EDS) to assess the oxide scale continuity and composition, and conduct mechanical tests (room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature tests at 1000 °C with strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
measurements: Surface oxide scale morphology and continuity (via microscopy/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not display a reduction in oxidation weight gain or improved oxide scale adherence and/or if its mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) deteriorate significantly relative to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. As mentioned above, the CoCrNi MEA has excellent comprehensive properties compared with other alloys. The addition of Al is conducive to the formation of a continuous oxide layer of the alloy and enhances the oxidation resistance of the matrix. At present, there are few studies on the Al-containing CoCrNi MEA prepared using powder metallurgy. In this study, Al-added CoCrNi MEAs were prepared using powder metallurgy mechanical alloying, and the effects of different Al contents on the mechanical properties and oxidation resistance of CoCrNi MEAs were investigated. The results show that the mechanical properties and oxidation resistance of CoCrNi MEAs were improved greatly and the mechanisms for these improvements are discussed. This study paves the way for future applications in high-temperature fields.

occupying_moves.lever: filling the gap in prior evaluations by focusing on equiatomic alloys rather than non-equiatomic or other refractory alloys
occupying_moves.technique: comparative analysis of oxidation behavior using microscopy and weight-gain measurements on equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with/without minor Al addition
occupying_moves.conditions: Standardized high-temperature oxidation test (air at ~800 °C for 5 h) coupled with mechanical testing to ensure no detrimental effects on ductility or strength

chosen.lever: alloy composition modification via addition of a small amount of Al
chosen.technique: arc-melting synthesis of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with ~2–4 at% Al, followed by conventional high-temperature oxidation testing
chosen.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours with subsequent mechanical evaluation at room temperature and at 1000 °C (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹)
chosen.why: This move directly targets the untested condition of the equiatomic alloy by adapting a proven oxidation-protection intervention from related non-equiatomic systems. The minor Al addition is expected to promote the formation of a continuous, protective alumina layer without compromising the alloy’s documented mechanical performance. The standard synthesis and testing protocols make this both a practical and impactful single intervention.
